options.misconception: confuses the nugget with the sill value

options.text: The offset above zero is the variance from repeated counts at one site.

options.misconception: reads a nugget as proof of no structure

options.text: The offset above zero means close sites disagree more than distant ones.
options.misconception: believes close sites must differ more

questions.explanation: A variogram starting above zero at zero separation carries a nugget, the variance produced by repeated measurement alone. Real structure still shows as the climb towards the sill, so the field is not unstructured.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What the cell size of a raster does and does not decide
questions.learningObjective: Design a controlled test of how cell size changes reported area
questions.stem: I want to know whether halving the pixel size of my sky survey frames changes the total woodland area I report, so I need a design for a fair test.

answer.exemplar: Reprocess the same set of scenes twice, once at the original cell size and once at half that size, keeping the classification rule, the training data and the ground truth identical in both runs. Then sum the woodland area in each run and compare the two totals, so that any difference can only come from the change in cell size.

questions.explanation: A fair test changes only the cell size, holding the scenes and classification rule fixed, then compares summed class areas. Mixed pixels bias coarse and fine results differently, so only like-for-like runs reveal the resolution effect.
questions.hint: Change one thing and hold the rest steady.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A vegetation index from red and near-infrared reflectance
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a red and near-infrared index separates vegetation from soil
questions.stem: Explain why a normalised difference vegetation index built from red and near-infrared reflectance separates bare soil from healthy green canopy.

answer.exemplar: Healthy green canopy reflects strongly in the near-infrared but absorbs red light for photosynthesis, so the two bands differ greatly and the index is large. Bare soil reflects red and near-infrared almost equally, so the difference stays near zero and the index remains low.

questions.explanation: The index divides the near-infrared minus red difference by their sum. Canopy reflects far more in the near-infrared than in the red, while soil reflects both nearly equally, so soil sits near zero.
questions.hint: Think about which band photosynthesis removes.

questions.stem: I estimate daily gross primary production for one meadow tile from a vegetation index of 0.75, daily radiation of 20 megajoules per square metre and a light use efficiency of 0.12 grams of carbon per megajoule.
questions.explanation: Index times radiation times efficiency: 0.75 times 20 is 15, and 15 times 0.12 is 1.8 grams of carbon per square metre per day. Dropping the efficiency would give 15, eight times too high.
questions.hint: Multiply the three factors in order.

options.misconception: treats the light ratio as the leaf index itself

options.text: My estimate is 0.2, since a fifth of the light is what reaches the floor.
options.misconception: reports the transmitted fraction as the index

options.misconception: compounds the ratio to get a squared leaf count

questions.explanation: The log rule converts a light ratio into a leaf index: natural log of five is about 1.61, so the canopy holds roughly 1.6 leaf layers. The fivefold loss is only a light ratio.

questions.explanation: The range is the separation at which the variogram plateaus, so beyond 30 km the sites hold no more information about each other. The sill is instead the variance value reached at that plateau.

questions.topic: Inverse distance weighting at an unsampled point
questions.learningObjective: Design a test of how sensitive interpolation is to the weighting power
questions.stem: I must design a check that shows how sensitive my interpolated brightness surface is to the distance weighting power I choose.

answer.exemplar: Interpolate the same unsampled cells at several powers, for example one, two and four, and record how far each predicted value moves from the value obtained at power one. Hold the input readings, the set of neighbours and the study area fixed so that only the weighting exponent differs, then compare the spread of the predictions with the spread of the observations themselves.

questions.explanation: Varying only the weighting power and watching the predictions move shows how sensitive the surface is to that choice. If the spread is small against the measurement noise, the choice hardly matters.
questions.hint: Change only the power and compare predictions.

questions.topic: A productivity model carried across a whole zone
questions.learningObjective: Design a test that separates model edge effects from real change
questions.stem: I must design a test that separates a real productivity trend across my survey zone from an artefact of how the model treats the zone edges.

answer.exemplar: Rerun the model on an inner zone that excludes the boundary tiles, leaving the classification inputs and the model settings unchanged, then compare the trend in the inner zone with the trend from the full zone. If the drop survives without the edge tiles it is a property of the field, and if it disappears the original signal was a boundary artefact of the model.

questions.explanation: Removing the boundary tiles and rerunning the same model tests whether the drop survives without edge cells, so a surviving drop points to real change while a vanishing one points to the boundary.
questions.hint: Take away the edge and see what remains.

questions.topic: Leaf area index from the light reaching the floor
questions.learningObjective: Explain why canopy light loss grows with leaf area index
questions.stem: Explain why the light reaching the forest floor falls as the leaf area index of a canopy rises.

answer.exemplar: Each extra layer of leaves intercepts a further fraction of the light passing through it, so the beam is attenuated again and again before it reaches the ground. Because the loss is multiplicative, a canopy with twice the leaf area index passes far less light, following a logarithmic decline rather than a linear one.

questions.explanation: Light is intercepted layer by layer, so each addition of foliage multiplies the loss rather than subtracting a fixed amount. The fall in transmitted light with leaf area index is therefore logarithmic, not linear.
questions.hint: Every layer takes a share of what remains.

questions.topic: A vegetation index from red and near-infrared reflectance
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of soil brightness on a vegetation index
questions.stem: Explain why a bright dry soil can push the vegetation index of a sparse shrub canopy higher than the canopy alone would suggest.

answer.exemplar: The index divides the near-infrared minus red difference by the sum of both bands, so bright dry soil raises the red and near-infrared readings together. questions.explanation: Bright dry soil adds similar amounts to both bands, so it inflates the denominator of the index without adding much to the numerator. On a sparse canopy that lifts the index above the value the vegetation supports.

questions.stem: Explain why a canopy with very dense foliage cannot be distinguished from a moderately dense one by its light transmission alone.

answer.exemplar: Once the canopy is dense enough, almost all the light is stopped high in the crown, so the extra leaves hanging below add little further attenuation. questions.explanation: In a dense canopy most light is stopped near the top, so extra leaves lower down barely change the transmitted fraction. The index then flattens and can no longer separate dense from moderately dense cover.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Class area from a count of image cells
questions.learningObjective: Explain why class areas depend on the choice of cell size
questions.stem: Explain why the woodland area I calculate from my map can change when I reprocess the same imagery at a finer cell size.

answer.exemplar: A cell holds one value for all the ground it covers, so at a coarse size a woodland edge cell mixes woodland with open ground and is counted as one or the other by a single decision. At a finer size those boundary cells are split into several smaller ones, and the boundary cells that get reassigned change slightly, which shifts the total mapped woodland area even though the ground itself is unchanged.

questions.explanation: Boundary cells mix classes, and their split between woodland and open ground changes with cell size, so the total class area moves even though the ground does not. Finer grids resolve the edge better but do not remove it.
questions.hint: Edge cells change their class as cells change.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What the cell size of a raster does and does not decide
questions.learningObjective: Compute the map area represented by a grid of cells
questions.stem: A classified tile of my survey is 25 cells wide and 16 cells tall at 20 metre resolution, and I need its total ground area in square kilometres.
questions.explanation: The tile spans 500 metres by 320 metres, which is 160 000 square metres, and dividing by a million square kilometres per square kilometre gives 0.16. Counting the 400 cells without the cell size would give no area.
questions.hint: Cell count times cell area, then convert units.
